title: Guarded lazy checkout routes
summary: Implement a functional checkout decision, then review a route table that eagerly loads checkout and never guards or titles it.

scenario.briefing: The checkout route ships in the initial bundle, opens with an empty cart, and leaves the old page title in the browser tab.

objectives.description: Implement a pure functional guard decision.
Review route configuration for access, loading, and accessibility.

hints: Return login for a signed-out visitor.
Return catalog for a signed-in visitor with no items.
Use loadComponent and a title on the checkout route.

misconceptions.description: Allowing checkout because the route exists.
misconceptions.testDescription: Signed-out visitors are sent to login.
misconceptions.feedback: A route that exists is not a route that is allowed. The guard must return login for a signed-out visitor.

misconceptions.description: Letting a signed-in visitor check out with no items.
misconceptions.testDescription: An empty cart is sent to the catalog.
misconceptions.feedback: Checkout with no items cannot complete. Redirect to the catalog so the user can add something first.

misconceptions.description: Accepting an eager, unguarded, untitled route.
misconceptions.feedback: Eager loading, missing authorization, and a stale title are production defects. The route table must change before release.

sections.title: A guard is a function
sections.body: A functional CanActivate guard returns true, false, or a UrlTree. Keep the decision pure so it can be tested without the router or a TestBed.

sections.title: Lazy routes shrink the first bundle
sections.body: loadComponent imports a standalone component only when the route activates. Eagerly importing checkout puts its code in the initial bundle for every visitor.

sections.title: Titles and focus are navigation
sections.body: A route title updates the browser and assistive technology. The app shell still has to move focus to the new heading after activation.

vocabulary.definition: A route guard written as a function instead of a class.
A route property that lazily imports a standalone component.
A route property that sets the document title after navigation.

steps.title: Decide checkout access
steps.prompt: Edit checkout.guard.ts. Return login for a signed-out visitor, catalog for an empty cart, and allow only when both conditions pass.
hints: Use signedIn as the first branch.
Check itemCount <= 0 in the second branch.
Return allow only after both checks pass.
Keep the return type so every branch is explicit.

steps.title: Review the route table
steps.prompt: Review app.routes.ts and select every real access, loading, or accessibility problem.
hints: Look for canActivate on the checkout route.
Check whether CheckoutComponent is imported at the top of the file.
Look for a title property on the route.
Reject findings that describe code the route table does not contain.

artifact.title: app.routes.ts
artifact.caption: Checkout is eagerly imported, has no guard, and declares no title.

findings.label: The checkout route has no canActivate guard, so an empty cart can open it.
CheckoutComponent is imported eagerly instead of with loadComponent, so it ships in the initial bundle.
The checkout route declares no title, so the browser tab keeps the previous page name.
A functional guard already protects the checkout route.
The route uses loadComponent for checkout.

verdicts.label: Block the change until the listed risks are fixed.
Ship it; the remaining concerns are cosmetic.
Only formatting and naming need work.

steps.explanation: The route has metadata but no guard, imports CheckoutComponent eagerly, and never sets a title. The data property alone does not enforce access or lazy loading.
